content: The second part of the document, titled Implementation Manual, provides detailed guidance on the application of standards for prosthetics and orthotics services. It is a technical contribution to the World Health Organization's (WHO) standards for prosthetics and orthotics, focusing on improving access to high-quality, affordable services. The manual is designed to assist Member States in analyzing their current situation, setting priorities, and implementing the standards effectively. The manual emphasizes the importance of collaboration among various stakeholders, including users, families, caregivers, user groups, disabled people's organizations, governments, civil society organizations, service providers, training institutions, manufacturers, and international organizations. Each stakeholder plays a complementary role in establishing and maintaining effective prosthetics and orthotics services. Service users, along with their families and caregivers, are central to the planning, implementation, monitoring, and evaluation of these services. Their involvement is not only a right but also a critical resource for ensuring that services meet their needs. User groups and organizations representing disabled individuals can advocate on behalf of users, participate in program planning and evaluation, and represent user interests on advisory committees. The manual also outlines the scope and structure of prosthetics and orthotics services, covering four core areas: policy (governance, financing, and information), products (prostheses and orthoses), personnel (workforce), and service provision. It provides advice on planning, implementing, managing, and improving these services to meet the proposed standards. The document encourages governments and national stakeholders to work together in a joint effort to plan, set goals, implement, and monitor services. The manual includes country examples to illustrate various topics and stimulate discussion on the wide range of issues involved in preparing policies, strategic plans, and benchmarks for services. However, it does not serve as a detailed blueprint for implementation in all countries, as plans and priorities vary depending on the context and available resources. The manual also addresses the importance of early detection and treatment of impairments, prevention of avoidable impairments, and ensuring cost-effectiveness in service delivery. It highlights the need for accessible services, user-centered policies, and the inclusion of prosthetics and orthotics services in the broader health sector. Additionally, it discusses the development of affordable products, regulation of technical issues, and the role of research in advancing the field. In terms of personnel, the manual emphasizes the need for training, continuing professional development, workforce planning, and retention of skilled professionals. It also underscores the importance of professional regulation, recognition, and the role of professional associations in supporting the workforce. The manual promotes the integration of prosthetics and orthotics services into health systems, decentralization of services, and the establishment of maintenance and repair services. It also addresses service provision in disaster settings and the management of service units, including equipment, working environments, and safety considerations. Overall, the manual serves as a comprehensive guide for Member States to improve prosthetics and orthotics services, ensuring that they are accessible, high-quality, and aligned with the needs of users. It encourages collaboration, innovation, and a user-centered approach to service delivery.
